title: Segmented export scheduler and metric mesh for low-latency flushes
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Under bursty traffic we see long exporter CPU spikes and tail latencies caused by a single monolithic OTLP export queue. High-cardinality traces and occasional large batches cause transient GC pressure and export stalls that violate p95 latency SLOs for interactive workloads.

Goal: Replace the single exporter queue with a segmented export scheduler (sharded by priority and tenant affinity) and add a lightweight metric mesh that dynamically tunes batch size and flush intervals. The change should reduce peak allocations and CPU during bursts, reduce p95 export latency, and provide observable backpressure signals for routing.

Proposed changes: 1) Segmented export scheduler: create multiple fixed-size export shards (control by config) that accept spans/metrics/logs routed by (priority, tenant hash mod N). Each shard has its own reuse pool for protobuf messages and holds a small ring buffer to avoid large contiguous allocations.
2) Adaptive flush controller (metric mesh): collect exporter_queue_depth, export_latency_p50/p95, export_error_rate and feed into a controller that increases/decreases batch_size and flush_interval per shard to meet a latency SLO. Controller uses exponential backoff on failure and additive increase on success to avoid oscillation.
3) Exporter connection pooling: reuse a small set of long-lived gRPC OTLP streams per region instead of per-shard short-lived connections. Implement round-robin and idempotent retry semantics.
4) Record-level filter pipeline: introduce configurable lightweight filters to drop or redact noisy high-cardinality attributes before encoding (rule engine with safe defaults).
5) Dependency upgrades and build regen: otel-sdk-go v1.20 -> v1.24, otlp-grpc exporter 0.19 -> 0.22, protoc-generated pb files regenerated with protoc v4.x, and upgrade internal protobuf helper.

Success metrics (target):
- Exporter p95 latency reduced by >= 30% under burst load.
- Peak heap allocations during export reduced by >= 40%.
- Exporter_queue_depth tail (p99) <= 3x baseline.
- No increase in successful export error rate > 0.5% above baseline.

Rollout plan:
- Feature gated behind runtime config (SEGMENTED_EXPORTER=true) and control-plane switch for Dedicated/Private customers.
- Canary: route 2% of traffic for 48h, monitor stable signals (export_latency_p95, gc_pause, failed_exports).
- Gradual ramp: 2% -> 10% -> 30% -> 100% with 24-48h observation windows.
- Automated rollback triggers: sustained export_latency_p95 increase > 20% for 1h or failed_export_rate > 1% for 30m.

Testing:
- Microbench: allocations and CPU for synthetic high-cardinality traces (10M spans/min) comparing old exporter and segmented scheduler.
- Integration: e2e test harness with otlp-gateway simulator that introduces variable latency and transient errors.
- Load staging: run a scaled staging cluster with canary traffic to validate metric mesh behavior and cluster-wide connection pooling.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Schema drift / consumer incompatibility from record-level filters. Mitigation: defaults are conservative (only drop attributes above cardinality threshold) and we provide opt-in filter rules per customer.
- Risk: Added complexity in shutdown paths could leak goroutines. Mitigation: add deterministic shard drain with timeout and unit tests for graceful stop.
- Risk: Upgrading otel SDK may subtly change sampling or semantic conventions. Mitigation: run a back-compat test suite that compares sampling decisions on deterministic inputs.

Artifacts & links:
- Design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/SEGMENTED-EXPORTER-2026
- Prototype benchmark results: https://internal-graphs.redwood.com/bench/segmented-exporter-2026-03-02
- GH prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/12812

Notes on trade-offs:
- We intentionally bias toward per-shard small ring buffers to limit large contiguous allocations; this slightly increases bookkeeping cost but yields large GC benefits.
- Connection pooling centralizes TCP resources which may slightly increase latency for low-volume tenants; we expose pooling knobs per-region.

Next steps:
- Finish proto reuse pool and unit tests (in progress).
- Wire metric mesh controller and add controller health metrics.
- Run 48h canary once PR is green and benchmarks hit targets.
comments: 2026-03-02 - Aisha Patel: Spiked a prototype with 4 shards + reuse pools. Initial microbench shows 37% lower allocs and 28% lower p95 export latency under a synthetic burst (10k spans/sec). Reused protos reduced GC churn noticeably.

2026-03-04 - Marco Rossi: Implemented adaptive flush controller loop and exposed metrics exporter_queue_depth, shard_flush_interval_seconds, shard_batch_size. Integration tests added. Observed one regression: a goroutine leak on shutdown when shard drains overlap; adding a shard-level context cancellation fixed it in local tests.

2026-03-06 - QA (Lina Gómez): Running e2e with otlp-gateway simulator. Found that connection pooling had a pathological retry loop when server returned UNAVAILABLE; added per-call retry cap and jitter to backoff. Filing follow-up ENG-91240 for retry tuning.

2026-03-08 - Infra (Kenji Tanaka): Noted increased FD usage in early prototype due to per-shard short-lived connections; switching to pooled channels reduced FD usage by ~60% in staging. Will validate under heavy tenancy.
2026-03-10 - PM (Riley Chen): Approved canary for 2% traffic starting 2026-03-12 pending GH PR merge and staging run results. PM asked that we add an SLO dashboard tile for the controller metrics.
